title: Learning with Agents
summary: The meta-map: how to learn anything with an AI agent beside you without letting it do the learning for you. Its two thresholds are generation before help, and calibrated metacognition: knowing what you know, measured rather than felt.
sources: Brown, Roediger, McDaniel: Make It Stick
Bastani et al.: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS, 2025)
Pashler et al.: Learning styles: concepts and evidence (2008)

nodes.label: Outcomes Before Content
nodes.summary: Decide what you will be able to do, in a verb you can test, before choosing what to read (backward design).
nodes.outcome: Rewrite a vague goal as a testable outcome.
nodes.check: Rewrite 'understand recursion' as a testable outcome.
nodes.answer: E.g. 'write a recursive function that sums a nested list, with a correct base case, unaided'.

nodes.label: Retrieval Practice
nodes.summary: Pulling knowledge out of memory strengthens it more than putting it in again (the testing effect).
nodes.outcome: Replace a re-reading session with a self-test session.
nodes.check: Which produces better retention a week later: re-reading a chapter twice, or reading once and self-testing?

nodes.label: "Re-reading is studying"
nodes.summary: Re-reading builds familiarity, which feels like knowing but does not survive a test.
nodes.outcome: Explain why familiarity is not recall.
nodes.answer: Processing fluency rises, which we mistake for learning (an illusion of competence).

nodes.label: Spacing
nodes.summary: Reviews spread over growing intervals beat the same reviews massed together.
nodes.outcome: Schedule reviews at expanding intervals (e.g. 1, 3, 7, 16 days).
nodes.check: Three hours of study: one block the night before, or three one-hour blocks across a week?

nodes.label: Interleaving
nodes.summary: Mixing problem types forces you to choose the method, which is the skill tests actually demand.
nodes.outcome: Design a mixed practice set across three topics.
nodes.check: Why does interleaved practice feel worse but test better?
nodes.answer: It is harder (a desirable difficulty) because you must discriminate which method applies.

nodes.label: Worked Examples & Fading
nodes.summary: Novices learn more from studying solutions than from solving; steps are then faded until they solve alone (Sweller).
nodes.outcome: Build a faded sequence: full example, partial example, solo problem.
nodes.check: For a complete novice, is it better to start with a worked example or an unaided problem?
nodes.answer: Usually a worked example (worked-example effect), unless deliberately designing productive failure.

nodes.label: Self-Explanation
nodes.summary: Explaining each step to yourself, especially why it follows, separates strong learners from weak ones (Chi).
nodes.outcome: Annotate a worked example with the reason for each step.
nodes.check: What question do you ask at each step of a worked example?
nodes.answer: 'Why does this step follow from the last?'

nodes.label: ICAP: Interactive > Constructive > Active > Passive
nodes.summary: Engagement modes ranked by learning: co-constructing with a partner beats generating alone beats manipulating beats receiving.
nodes.outcome: Classify a study activity by ICAP mode and upgrade it one level.
nodes.check: Highlighting a textbook is which ICAP mode?
nodes.answer: Active (manipulating material without generating anything new).

nodes.label: Generation Before Help
nodes.summary: Attempt first, ask second. An answer you generated, even wrongly, prepares you to learn from the correct one. This is the threshold for learning with an agent: the tool becomes a partner rather than an answer machine.
nodes.outcome: Commit a written attempt and a confidence rating before asking an agent.
nodes.check: Before asking an agent to solve a problem, what should you write down?
nodes.answer: Your own attempt (or prediction) and how confident you are in it.

nodes.label: "Asking the agent for the answer saves time"
nodes.summary: In a field experiment, students with unrestricted chatbot access did better on practice and worse on the unaided exam; a tutor-mode version with hints only removed the harm (Bastani et al.).
nodes.outcome: Set up an agent in hint-only mode for a practice session.
nodes.check: What did unguarded AI help do to unaided exam scores in Bastani et al.?
nodes.answer: It lowered them, even though practice scores rose.

nodes.label: Productive Failure
nodes.summary: Struggling with a problem before instruction, then consolidating, beats instruction first for conceptual transfer (Kapur).
nodes.outcome: Design a struggle phase followed by consolidation.
nodes.check: What must follow the failure phase for it to be productive?
nodes.answer: Consolidation: comparing attempts with the canonical solution.

nodes.label: The Hint Ladder
nodes.summary: Help in rungs: a question, then a pointer, then a sub-goal, then a worked step, never the whole answer first (Pólya; cognitive tutors).
nodes.outcome: Write a four-rung hint ladder for one problem.
nodes.check: What is the first rung of a good hint ladder?
nodes.answer: A question that redirects attention, e.g. 'What is the unknown?'

nodes.label: Explain-Back (Feynman Technique)
nodes.summary: Explain it in plain words to a novice; the places you reach for jargon are the gaps.
nodes.outcome: Explain a concept in under 150 plain words and mark the gaps.
nodes.check: What signals a gap during explain-back?
nodes.answer: Reaching for jargon or skipping a step you cannot justify.

nodes.label: Calibrated Metacognition
nodes.summary: Knowing what you know, measured: confidence ratings checked against results. Most learners are overconfident after easy study.
nodes.outcome: Track confidence versus correctness over a set and compute calibration.
nodes.check: You were 90% confident on 10 answers and got 6 right. What does that say?
nodes.answer: You are overconfident: 60% accuracy at 90% confidence.

nodes.label: "I'm a visual learner"
nodes.summary: Matching instruction to a preferred 'learning style' has no supporting evidence (Pashler et al.). Match the mode to the content instead.
nodes.outcome: Choose a representation by what the content is.
nodes.check: Should a map of a city be taught as text to an 'auditory learner'?
nodes.answer: No: the content is spatial, so a map serves everyone.

nodes.label: Deliberate Practice
nodes.summary: Effortful practice at the edge of ability with immediate feedback on specific sub-skills (Ericsson).
nodes.outcome: Design a practice block targeting one weak sub-skill with feedback.
nodes.check: What separates deliberate practice from repetition?
nodes.answer: A specific target just beyond current ability, focused effort, and immediate feedback.

nodes.label: Verifying Agent Output
nodes.summary: Every claim an agent makes is a hypothesis: run it, derive it, or find the source.
nodes.outcome: Verify an agent's derivation by an independent route.
nodes.check: An agent gives a formula. Name two independent checks.
nodes.answer: Dimensional analysis and a limiting or special case (or a numeric test).

nodes.label: Far Transfer
nodes.summary: Using knowledge in a context unlike the one it was learned in: the real test of understanding.
nodes.outcome: Solve a problem from a different domain with a learned principle.
nodes.check: Why are textbook end-of-chapter problems a weak test of transfer?
nodes.answer: The chapter heading tells you which method to use.
